title: Subordinate clauses 1
subtitle: dat, omdat, als, toen, terwijl, hoewel: the verb goes to the end

lessons.title: dat, omdat, of: verb at the end

explain.text: A **subordinate clause** cannot stand alone. It starts with a word like **dat** (that), **omdat** (because) or **of** (whether), and **all verbs go to the end** of the clause. The subject comes right after the conjunction: *Ik denk **dat hij morgen komt**.* *Ik blijf thuis, **omdat het koud is**.*
A **separable verb** becomes one word again at the end of the clause: *Ik bel je op* → *Ik weet dat zij morgen **opbelt**.*

explain.nl: Ik weet dat zij morgen opbelt.
explain.en: I know that she is going to phone tomorrow.

explain.nl: Weet jij of de winkel open is?
explain.en: Do you know whether the shop is open?

explain.text: Check the verb: *dat hij komt*, never *dat hij komt morgen*. The conjugated verb is the very last word.

explain.text: More subordinating words, all with the verb at the end. **Als** = *if* or *whenever* (present, future or a habit). **Toen** = *when*, for **one moment in the past**. **Wanneer** = *when* in questions and formal speech.

explain.text: **Toen** is only for the past. For the present or the future, and for habits, use **als**: *Als ik moe ben, ga ik slapen.*

explain.text: A subordinate clause can also come **first**. Then the whole clause counts as the first element of the sentence, so the **main clause starts with its verb** (inversion): *Als het regent, **blijf ik** thuis.* The two verbs meet at the comma.
